final_proof:
Interpret the half-open interval in the statement as \(( -\pi,\pi]\), which is the endpoint convention consistent with the displayed formula. Also, the real arctangent has domain \(\mathbb R\) and takes its values in \(( -\pi/2,\pi/2)\); the latter interval is its range.

For a nonzero vector \(\mathbf a=(x,y)\), put
\[
r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0.
\]
Its direction angle is the unique \(\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\) satisfying
\[
(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=\left(\frac{x}{r},\frac{y}{r}\right). \tag{1}
\]
Uniqueness follows from the standard fact that two real angles with the same sine and cosine differ by an integral multiple of \(2\pi\), since no two distinct points of the half-open interval \(( -\pi,\pi]\) differ by \(2\pi\).

First suppose \(x\ne0\), and set
\[
\alpha=\arctan\left(\frac yx\right).
\]
By the definition of the principal real arctangent,
\[
-\frac\pi2<\alpha<\frac\pi2,\qquad \tan\alpha=\frac yx,\qquad \cos\alpha>0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\cos\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt{1+\tan^2\alpha}}=\frac{|x|}{r},\qquad \sin\alpha=\tan\alpha\cos\alpha=\frac{y}{x}\frac{|x|}{r}. \tag{2}
\]

If \(x>0\), equation (2) gives \((\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)=(x/r,y/r)\). Moreover, \(\alpha\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\subset(-\pi,\pi]\). Thus (1) and uniqueness show that
\[
\theta=\alpha=\arctan(y/x).
\]

Now suppose \(x<0\). Then (2) gives
\[
(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)=(-x/r,-y/r). \tag{3}
\]
Using \(\cos(t\pm\pi)=-\cos t\) and \(\sin(t\pm\pi)=-\sin t\), either \(\alpha+\pi\) or \(\alpha-\pi\) therefore satisfies (1). It remains only to select the representative in \(( -\pi,\pi]\).

If additionally \(y\ge0\), then \(y/x\le0\), so \(\alpha\in(-\pi/2,0]\). Hence
\[
\alpha+\pi\in(\pi/2,\pi]\subset(-\pi,\pi],
\]
and therefore
\[
\theta=\alpha+\pi=\arctan(y/x)+\pi.
\]
This includes \(y=0\), for which \(\theta=\pi\), as required by the chosen half-open convention. If instead \(y<0\), then \(y/x>0\), so \(\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)\), and
\[
\alpha-\pi\in(-\pi,-\pi/2)\subset(-\pi,\pi].
\]
Thus
\[
\theta=\alpha-\pi=\arctan(y/x)-\pi.
\]

It remains to consider \(x=0\). If \(y>0\), then \(r=y\), so the normalized vector in (1) is \((0,1)\), whose representative in \(( -\pi,\pi]\) is \(\theta=\pi/2\). If \(y<0\), then \(r=-y\), so the normalized vector is \((0,-1)\), whose representative is \(\theta=-\pi/2\).

Finally, if \(x=y=0\), then \(\mathbf a\) is the zero vector. It cannot be written as \(r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) with \(r>0\), and rotating it does not distinguish any direction. Hence its direction is undefined. These cases give exactly the asserted formula.
